`resize`: set or show the terminal's size.

## Synopsis

<strong>resize</strong> \[<strong>-s</strong> <em>rows</em> <em>columns</em>\]

## Description

<strong>resize</strong> asks the terminal how big it is, tells the kernel (so the program in front gets SIGWINCH, and looks again), and prints shell commands setting <strong>COLUMNS</strong> and <strong>LINES</strong>, for <strong>eval</strong>.

A terminal powers on at the largest its tier shows: 50 by 16 (tier 1), 80 by 25 (tier 2), 160 by 50 (tier 3). It can be made smaller, and larger again up to that. In the console's group (every screen the console shows on), the largest is what every one of them can show, and they're all the same size.

## Options

<strong>-s</strong> <em>rows columns</em>
: First asks the terminal to be <em>rows</em> by <em>columns</em> (xterm's sequence, <strong>ESC\[8;</strong>rows<strong>;</strong>columns<strong>t</strong>), no larger than it can be; <strong>0</strong> is the largest. Text that no longer fits is dropped (lines above the cursor go into the scrollback first), and nothing is wrapped again.

## Exit status

0 on success; 1 for a bad argument, or when the terminal didn't answer.

## Examples

```text
resize -s 25 80
resize -s 0 0
eval $(resize)
```

## Notes

As xterm's, it talks to its terminal with escape sequences through <strong>/dev/tty</strong>: a program can do the same (<strong>ESC\[18t</strong> asks the size, <strong>ESC\[19t</strong> the largest). A program that resizes the terminal itself, without telling the kernel, leaves the program in front unaware until it asks again.

## See also

<strong>stty</strong>(1)
